articles.title_orig: Lowry: Jensen Huang and the great Chinese heist
articles.title_zh: Lowry: Jensen Huang and the great Chinese heist
articles.content_orig:
Syndicated and guest columns represent the personal views of the writers, not necessarily those of the editorial staff. The editorial department operates entirely independently of the news department and is not involved in newsroom operations.
There have been surprises in the Nvidia saga — not least the shocking return of Jensen Huang — but what's unsurprising is that China was using underhanded means to acquire U.S. technology. This is a core competency of the Chinese state.
The effort began upon the normalization between the United States and China in 1979, as the Chinese immediately set about ripping off McDonnell Douglas technology to improve their military aircraft. The scale of China's theft of U.S. intellectual property over the decades is almost unfathomable, and it's an ongoing, comprehensive campaign of the Chinese government.
China's spy agency, the Ministry of State Security, employs as many as 800,000 people by one estimate, an appropriately gargantuan enterprise for a totalitarian state with sweeping international reach and ambitions.
Although it's a matter of debate whether Jensen Huang's love interest, Alice Huang, was a formal "spy," she was in touch with an officer of the Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until this fall, according to a New York Times report. Evidence suggests that her business partner and, as The Times puts it, the man "who was often introduced as her husband," Kang Wei, worked with the agency.
Alice Huang was associated with a business called Megaspeed that used Nvidia chips in data centers in Southeast Asia, giving Chinese concerns remote access to them. It also may have been part of a smuggling operation to send semiconductors to China. For his part, Kang was creating a $9 billion Chinese data-center network backed by the government.
They were thus at the center of a business of the highest interest to the Chinese spy agency. It has made "counterblockade" work one of its top priorities, assisting Chinese companies in acquiring and smuggling advanced chips.
Chen Yixin, the head of the ministry, has written of the agency's mission to "deepen the struggle against blockades, and comprehensively advance artificial intelligence innovation, industry development, and applications." In other words, the Ministry of State Security would be falling down on the job if it didn't have its hooks into Alice Huang and her business partner, as it does in so many others.
The National Intelligence Law of 2017 imposed an obligation on all Chinese citizens and organizations to cooperate in intelligence work. It's as if the United States adopted a rule mandating that all Americans cooperate with the CIA.
The decades-long Chinese heist has been multifaceted. It has involved cybertheft, leveraging Chinese employees in the United States to pass along information, learning know-how from the U.S. employees of Chinese subsidiaries, using Chinese academic institutions and students to penetrate U.S. companies, exploiting joint ventures, physically stealing technology, investing in and buying U.S. companies or manufacturing their products, and, of course, using every possible means to pressure U.S. entities into sharing intellectual property to gain access to the Chinese market.
All of this has been enormously successful. David Shedd, the former acting director of the Defense Intelligence Agency, calls it "the greatest transfer of illicit wealth in human history."
It is one thing to potentially lose a technological competition to a rival power that is more talented and innovative; it is another to fall behind a competitor that relies on state-supported theft to gain the upper hand, taking advantage of our naivete and openness.
What to do? In a 2025 report, the Information Technology & Innovation Foundation recommends pre-emption as the best tool to counter the Chinese. U.S. companies need to better understand their vulnerabilities and bolster their defenses, while we should, among other things, be blacklisting Chinese universities whose students are involved in industrial espionage, and monitoring and restricting Chinese investment and R&D in the United States.
We all know the famous quote attributed to Lenin, "The capitalists will sell us the rope with which we will hang them." The Chinese version implicitly adds that whatever rope we don't sell, they will steal through any means necessary.
Rich Lowry is on X @RichLowry.

articles.title_orig: Two Italians killed in Kuwait as a strained Iran ramps up attacks
articles.title_zh: Two Italians killed in Kuwait as a strained Iran ramps up attacks
articles.content_orig:
Two Italians have died from their injuries in Kuwait, after being hit by falling debris as authorities said they tried to intercept incoming Iranian drones.
Kuwait’s Ministry of Defence said two other workers, a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national, were also wounded in the incident, at what the ministry describes as a “vital site”.
However, Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi held a phone conversation with his Kuwaiti counterpart Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, denying Tehran’s involvement and saying Tehran was prepared to conduct a “joint investigation with the Kuwaiti side” into the incident, state TV reported.
“During the call, Araghchi firmly rejected allegations regarding an Iranian drone attack on Kuwait, stating that the Islamic Republic of Iran had no involvement whatsoever,” it said.
Iran’s military spokesman Sardar Shekarchi said there had been “no offensive or military operations in the region”, and said that “given the history of hostile actions and the role of the Zionist regime and American forces in using false flags and regional adventures, these accusations are considered a cover for continuing evil and an attempt to increase insecurity in the region”.
Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation confirmed its citizens’ deaths, saying, “an explosion caused by a drone attack … occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working,” with Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirming the victims were technicians working at an air-defence surveillance station.
“Regarding the targeting of a vital site in the country as a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, the two injured Italian nationals have died as a result of their injuries,” said Kuwait’s Defence Ministry. It had earlier said the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified “material damage”.
Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi said the Iranian drone attack happened while the Kuwaiti National Guard and Kuwaiti military were meeting with an Italian delegation that was visiting, including the commander general of the Italian Carabinieri, Lieutenant-General Salvatore Lungo, as well as the Italian ambassador to Kuwait.
Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was informed of the “tragic deaths”.
“On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims’ families,” Meloni wrote on X.
The countries of the Gulf region “have in one voice said an attack against one is an attack against all and have continued to condemn these attacks as a violation of sovereignty”, but we’ve seen an uptick in attacks since September, said Basravi, reporting from Doha.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned Thursday’s “brutal” attack.
In a statement, Albudaiwi stressed that Iran’s continued attacks on Kuwait, targeting its vital facilities and endangering the lives of civilians, constitute a dangerous escalation and threaten regional security.
There was no immediate comment from Iran regarding the attack.
But it was in line with Tehran’s “policy change”, said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from the Iranian capital.
“Increasingly we have heard from the Iranian officials … saying that this state of no war, no peace cannot remain in place forever, and Iran is working on some military options … to break the status quo,” said Serdar.
The conflict – which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February – has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.
The United States and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran’s attempts to close the strait.
Thursday’s deadly attack comes days after Kuwait activated its air defences to counter drone strikes launched by Iran – the first since early September.

articles.title_orig: Hamas in talks with Palestinian factions over Israeli targeted killings in Gaza
articles.title_zh: Hamas in talks with Palestinian factions over Israeli targeted killings in Gaza
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in near daily air strikes over the past month
A Hamas political official and his wife were among eight Palestinians killed in three Israeli air strikes across the Gaza Strip on Thursday.
Local sources told the BBC a residential apartment in Deir al-Balah was targeted at dawn, killing Khaled Abu Nada - the deputy education minister - and his wife, Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada.
A Hamas Civil Defence spokesman said that rescue teams and medical personnel had transferred eight bodies to Al-Aqsa Hospital in central Gaza and Al-Shifa Hospital in Gaza City.
In a joint statement, Israel's prime minister and defence minister said the operation was "part of a series of targeted killings" against Hamas officials.
Thursday's strikes also reportedly killed three Palestinians on al-Nafaq Street, east of Gaza City. Their identities have not yet been established, eyewitnesses said.
In a separate strike on Shati refugee camp, west of Gaza City, three Palestinians working for Hamas's security services were killed. They were identified as Yasser al-Lahham, Iyad Ahmed and Ibrahim al-Mashal.
Khaled Abu Nada and his wife Abeer Mohammed Ismail Abu Nada were killed in the air strike
In a post X, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu confirmed the death of Khaled Abu Nada and said about 80 Hamas officials have been killed in the last month.
"No one in Hamas's leadership will succeed in evading us," he said, adding that the military would "continue to pursue our enemies and protect the security of Israeli civilians".
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had carried out a strike on a "senior" Hamas operative, and would provide further details later.
The attacks came a day after Mohammed Abu al-Ouf, 47, the head of Hamas's internal security service in northern Gaza, his wife and their two teenage daughters were killed in Israeli air strike on their apartment in Shati refugee camp in Gaza City.
On Tuesday, the overall commander of Hamas's internal security service was among 10 Palestinians reportedly killed in Israeli strikes.
Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under Hamas's control, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.
At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.
Israel says six of its soldiers have been killed in Gaza during the same period.
The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.
Since then, more than 74,772 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

articles.title_orig: Trump demands investigation into GDP data revisions
articles.title_zh: Trump demands investigation into GDP data revisions
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."
Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate . That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.
That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post , suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections , where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships.
"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.
However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.
On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.
The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.
Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary . Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.
GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.
The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.
Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.
Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."
"The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.
Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool . They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.
— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

articles.title_orig: Amtrak ridership hits record as high gas prices drive more Americans to train travel
articles.title_zh: Amtrak ridership hits record as high gas prices drive more Americans to train travel
articles.content_orig:
Union Pacific CEO Jim Vena and Union Pacific engineer Tom Moses join FOX Business reporter Grady Trimble in Northlake, Illinois, to discuss the proposed $85 billion railroad merger.
Amtrak said this week that it hit a record 37.1 million riders over the past year, a 7.4% jump fueled in part by Americans ditching expensive flights and high gas prices.
For the 12-month period ending Sept. 30, the rail service brought in $4.1 billion in total operating revenue, up 4.9% from the previous year. The company posted an adjusted net loss of $492.7 million — a 19% improvement over the previous year.
It marks the third straight year of record-breaking passenger volume for the rail operator.
"I have no doubt that the airline prices, gas prices pushed people to say, 'Maybe I should ride the train instead'," interim President Byl Herrmann said in an interview.
HOLIDAY AIRFARES HIT HIGHEST LEVELS IN A DECADE AS JET FUEL PRICES SURGE
Amtrak said Tuesday that it hit a record 37.1 million riders over the past year. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
He said significant infrastructure investments in the northeast corridor were key to improving reliability and boosting ridership as are new more reliable trainsets, which in some cases will replace trains that are more than 40 years old.
Amtrak plans to replace its northeast regional trainsets by 2028 and last year began replacing its higher-speed Acela trains with new trainsets.
"Frankly, I want to be in a range where I'm competing with the airlines, and some of these airlines, we're going to surpass them in the next few years for the number of passengers they have," Herrmann said.
THANKSGIVING TRAVEL TO DIP FOR FIRST TIME IN YEARS AS HIGHER COSTS WEIGH ON AMERICANS
Amtrak plans to replace its northeast regional trainsets by 2028 and last year began replacing its higher-speed Acela trains with new trainsets. (Jason Redmond/Reuters)
One of Amtrak's goals is to cut the journey between New York and Washington on its higher-speed Acela trains to just two-and-a-half hours, from around three hours or so currently.
Herrmann said that could happen by 2028 if the company gets approval to operate its new trains at higher speeds and makes fewer stops.
"If you're booking your trip, and you can do it in two and a half hours consistently, then you know that you can meet that meeting or that dinner reservation," Herrmann said.
Amtrak has received about $2.4 billion in annual government funding in recent years – on top of $22 billion approved in 2021 over five years for major projects.
Herrmann said Amtrak is hoping Congress would consider multi-year funding awards. "The ability to plan with only a one-year budget cycle is extraordinarily difficult," he said.
TSA ANTICIPATES NEARLY 18 MILLION AIR TRAVELERS DURING THANKSGIVING WEEK
One of Amtrak's goals is to cut the journey between New York and Washington on its higher-speed Acela trains. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call Inc via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The push to modernize comes as steep airline ticket prices continue to drive travelers toward alternative options. Americans traveling this holiday season are facing some of the highest airfares in a decade due to the surge in jet fuel prices earlier this year stemming from the Iran war.
"Airfare this holiday travel season will be the most expensive it's been in at least 10 years, and that's primarily coming as a result of jet fuel prices, which are two times higher than they were at this time last year as the conflict in Iran keeps fuel prices very high," Hayley Berg, lead economist at Hopper, previously told FOX business.
Reuters and FOX Business' Eric Revell contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft: Salt Typhoon’s ARTEX wins access ‘in a matter of minutes’
articles.title_zh: Microsoft: Salt Typhoon’s ARTEX wins access ‘in a matter of minutes’
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft logo at the Microsoft Experience Center, New York
State-backed hacking groups from China and North Korea, including Salt Typhoon, have added the AI attack framework ARTEX to their tools, Microsoft says. Microsoft Threat Intelligence named the groups in a report published on Wednesday .
The list covers Crystal Typhoon and Salt Typhoon, two Chinese state groups, and Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet, which Microsoft tracks as North Korean. Two more clusters, Storm-0940 and Storm-3358, are also on it. Microsoft says state-sponsored and financially motivated hackers use ARTEX to speed up network scans, credential attacks, and attacks on web apps.
“Depending on the threat actor’s configuration and the target’s defenses, ARTEX can advance from reconnaissance to persistent, privileged access to a target organization in a matter of minutes,” Microsoft wrote.
The report landed hours after US media tied ARTEX to the hack of three US spy agencies , as Jonathan Greig reported for The Record .
US agencies believe Salt Typhoon breached at least nine telecoms groups in 2024, The Record noted. That hack allegedly reached phones used by Donald Trump and JD Vance. A US House report later said Chinese carriers were still inside American phone networks .
Crystal Typhoon is newer. It was first seen in late 2023 and goes after government networks and critical infrastructure through edge devices and firewalls, TechRadar reported .
Microsoft had already linked Storm-0940 to the ConnectWise supply chain attack . The new report adds numbers from its campaigns. In one, Microsoft logged more than 151,000 failed sign-ins, peaking at 2,900 a minute. In several intrusions, the attackers had privileged access less than three hours after they first went after a target.
In another case, an AI agent went from searching GitHub for client secrets to taking data from Azure Key Vault in five minutes.
A GitHub user called Autumn-27 published ARTEX as open-source code with a Chinese interface in July. The developer took it down in October, but other developers kept publishing their own versions. This month, the Chinese security firm ThreatBook claimed ownership and started selling access to “ARTEX Pro”.
The attacker sets the targets. One AI model breaks the job into goals. A planner agent then hands short tasks to worker agents with a real shell and hacking tools. A reporter agent writes up what worked. ARTEX can run on almost any large language model, including ones stripped of their guardrails. That means no single AI provider’s safety controls can stop it, Microsoft says.
The FBI warned about ARTEX earlier this month.
“ARTEX does not introduce new attack techniques; it uses common, pre-existing penetration testing tools and techniques,” Microsoft wrote.
Attackers can change the tool’s IP addresses and user agent strings, so blocking those alone will not work. The steadiest sign is behaviour: many varied requests in a short burst, and quick moves to the next step. ARTEX does nothing to hide that activity by default.
Microsoft also suggests honeypots, tarpits, and fake wins. A fake win shows the agent false proof that its job is done, so it stops. It recommends rate limits, phishing-resistant multifactor sign-in, and replacing any secret that leaks into code. The report also points customers to Microsoft’s own products, including Defender XDR and its Perception security agents.

articles.title_orig: Ubisoft Wants Rayman To Become A Huge, Transmedia Star
articles.title_zh: Ubisoft Wants Rayman To Become A Huge, Transmedia Star
articles.content_orig:
Ubisoft is gearing up to launch Rayman Legends Retold , a reimagined remake of the 2013 original . While many have questioned the decision to remake a game that arguably still looks and plays great to this day, the developers have been clear in their intention to use Retold as a launchpad for the future of the franchise.
Now, in a new interview with The Game Business , brand producer Loïc Gounon has expressed much broader ambitions for the character, perhaps bringing Rayman more in line with something like Sonic in terms of visibility.
In other words, Gounon is thinking about not only games, but other mediums too, including TV shows and comics. The first step is to ensure the brand's success in regions such as the US and Asia, with previous Rayman titles' success being largely limited to Europe.
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
“I would like to see Rayman as a must-have IP for video games across the world. Rayman was generally stronger in France and the UK, and in some cases in the US. Enlarging the reach of the IP, also towards Asia and performing well in the US, is the first ambition… making sure that we are a must-have platforming adventure title across those markets in the video game world.
“And I guess beyond the video game world. So, comics, TV series... actually, there’s a French comic book that came out with Rabbids and Rayman being reconnected.”
However, Gounon does not necessarily believe that producing a new 3D title is the key to success, and instead wants to focus on the characters and lore. Sorry to those hoping for Rayman 4 – hey, it might still happen!
“Rayman is iconic because of its gameplay. But going back to the adventure roots of Rayman, having people dive into those characters, exploring deeper into that world and mythology, that’s what we believe in.
“It’s the world-building part, the consistency of that world-building, and the empathy for those characters, that will make the franchise last and maybe become bigger.”
Rayman Legends Retold is right around the corner, scheduled to launch on 3rd December 2026 . Meanwhile, Ubisoft itself is currently coming under fire for its heavy focus on generative AI , with a new report revealing that employees are required to justify reasons for not using the technology in new project pitches.

articles.title_orig: Net Migration to U.K. Falls to Lowest Level Since 1997, Excluding Pandemic
articles.title_zh: Net Migration to U.K. Falls to Lowest Level Since 1997, Excluding Pandemic
articles.content_orig:
Net migration to the UK has fallen to 77,000 in the year to the end of June - the lowest level this century, other than during the pandemic, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures show.
Excluding the limited movements of people during the worldwide travel restrictions in 2020, the figures show the number of people arriving in the UK, minus those leaving, tumbled 92% from the record high of 944,000 in the year to March 2023.
The ONS said this was the lowest net migration since 1997.
Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added  to the population in a given year.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the figures showed there was now "a sufficient degree of control" over the migration system.
The prime minister went on to say: "I'm not going to say all of the work is done, and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally as a country getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."
The underlying official statistics show that an estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said the figures showed that Labour had "delivered" after Conservative failures - but Chris Philp, her Tory shadow, said restrictions introduced by his party before the 2024 General Election were behind the falls.
The 77,000 figure is also the first time the UK has seen net migration in the tens of thousands since former PM David Cameron's controversial pledge 16 years ago to reach such a level.
The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.
These number had been expected to fall because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.
The effect of those policies, plus emigration from the UK, has meant that while net migration had already begun to fall, it more than halved in the last 12 months alone.
Mahmood said the figures showed the government had "restored control".
"We have brought net migration to 77,000, down 92% from its peak under the Conservatives," she said. "Where they failed, we have delivered for the British people."
This is a reference to the so-called "Boriswave" after Brexit. When the UK left the EU and its freedom of movement rules, Boris Johnson's government allowed in many more people to work and study from other parts of the world.
That led to the record-breaking arrivals in the year to March 2023. Johnson's successor, Rishi Sunak, introduced major restrictions on visas in the last months of his government.
Shadow home secretary Chris Philp said the falls were a result of those changes.
In a post on X, he called for an "annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels".
Dr Ben Brindle of Oxford University's Migration Observatory, an impartial expert body, said: "We are entering an unusual period where immigration has come down and may still have further to fall - but we still have relatively high emigration, at least for the time being.
"Most of those emigrants are non-citizens, including people who arrived a few years ago when immigration was very high. That could push the net migration figures down even further next year, but the downwards blip is unlikely to last forever."
In the year to June some 73,000 people arriving in the UK seeking asylum - down from 93,000 the previous year.
As of September, the number of people who were waiting for a decision was 41,000, down 49% on the previous year.
The Home Office said that these changes were driven by speeding up the system in taking decisions and a fall in the arrivals of new claimants via  "illegal entry routes" - largely meaning English Channel small boats.
As a result, the number of people accommodated in September by the Home Office was 93,000 - 16% lower than the year before. Some 52 hotels that had been dedicated to asylum seekers have been emptied this year. While some 140 are still in use the total number of people in hotels has fallen 64% to 13,000.
Responding to the latest statistics, Reform UK's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf said the figures were "no cause for celebration".
"This population explosion is why British people struggle to get a GP appointment, can't get housing and our prisons are overwhelmed."
Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesperson Paul Kohler said: "Britain faces serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services."
A spokesperson for the Green Party added: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and people seeking asylum is not a measure of success. The British people are overwhelmingly compassionate and will not be taken in by the dangerous and opportunistic narratives of the far right."

articles.title_orig: Lawmakers Seek AI Oversight, Tighter China Chip Controls
articles.title_zh: Lawmakers Seek AI Oversight, Tighter China Chip Controls
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia chip sellers are seeking new buyers for the semiconductor giant's hardware, three people told CNBC, after the Trump administration tightened rules to curb Chinese companies' remote access to the most advanced artificial-intelligence systems.
Companies have put an unusually high volume of Nvidia graphics processing units, or GPUs, on the market since new measures restricting Chinese companies renting access to advanced Nvidia chips were announced on Nov. 16, the people said.
Jack Duhamel, president of AI infrastructure marketplace GPU Mart, and two people familiar with the matter told CNBC the surge in GPUs for sale was directly attributable to the new rule. Duhamel added that one company looking to sell Nvidia chips told GPU Mart the sale was related to the new rule.
The two people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload them because they were originally for use in data centers in which Chinese companies would rent access. They asked not to be named because they were discussing private information.
The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced an interim final rule as part of a clampdown on Chinese companies bypassing export controls, which effectively ban the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to China, by accessing them remotely in overseas data centers. The rule came into effect on Nov. 19.
Deals to find buyers for thousands of B300 GPUs, one of Nvidia's most advanced offerings, have been floated since the rule was announced, said Duhamel and one of the people.
Nvidia declined to comment. BIS did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia has been facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips.
The chip giant warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.
In July, the U.S. accused a Chinese AI lab, Moonshot AI , of accessing Nvidia chips via a facility in Thailand. CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that the company had sought access to the chips via data centers in Europe.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new rule announced last week was intended to close "loopholes."
"For a long time, we have not allowed the sale of Blackwell chips, which are the highest AI chips or similar chips to China directly," he said.
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries."
During Nvidia's third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 17, then-interim CEO Colette Kress said the company was still studying the controls, but expected performance to remain strong because demand for chips far exceeded supply.

articles.title_orig: Spanish economist to become new European Central Bank chief
articles.title_zh: Spanish economist to become new European Central Bank chief
articles.content_orig:
The president of the European Council says eurozone member states have agreed to recommend Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the new European Central Bank (ECB) president.
Antonio Costa also announced that Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier have been recommended as members of the ECB executive board, and noted that this paves the way for the formal appointment of the new European Central Bank leadership by December’s European Union summit.
Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the first Spaniard to take the role, and succeeds France’s Christine Lagarde at the Frankfurt-based institution at a challenging time for the eurozone.
Currently head of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Basel-based forum for the world’s major central banks, the 55-year-old will take over in February, when Lagarde would step down several months before her term expires in October next year.
Thursday’s green light triggers a formal process during which European leaders will later in the day approve the candidates for each ECB post. The bank’s governing council and European Parliament will then formally back the nominations.
Diplomats have described the Spanish economist as a “steady hand” to steer the institution, with a reputation for pragmatism and consensus-building.
As the Bank of Spain’s chief economist and later governor, he navigated the aftermath of Spain’s 2010s banking crisis, years of ultra-low inflation, COVID-19 and the 2022 inflation surge that followed the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
He also chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for banks.
Spain’s Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who is battling unfavourable polling before a general election on Sunday, hailed the choice on social media, saying it reflects “a Spain that leads in Europe”.
He pointed to the Spanish chief of the European Investment Bank, Nadia Calvino, and the EU executive’s second-most senior official, Teresa Ribera, as other figures of influence.

articles.title_zh: China opposes proposed US tariffs
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer and President Trump speak to reporters aboard Air Force One. Photo: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/AFP via Getty Images
The Trump administration proposed a new round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union and 12 other economies over policies it says have created excess industrial capacity.
Why it matters: Trump officials are pressing ahead with his trade agenda despite a Democratic midterm sweep fueled by affordability concerns.
Driving the news: The tariffs are the result of  a trade investigation that launched in March , The proposed tariffs are a narrower approach than the sweeping import levies the administration has previously imposed, a senior U.S. official said.
Between the lines: The administration proposed tariffs of up to 20% to 35% on other targeted economies, though lower rates apply to trading partners with deals in place.
The big picture: The investigation was conducted under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The administration contends that foreign industrial policies encourage companies to produce more goods than global demand can absorb, undercutting U.S. manufacturers.
What they're saying: In response to reports of the proposed tariffs , China dismissed U.S. claims of industrial overcapacity as a "false proposition" and urged Washington to preserve stable trade relations.
Of note: The U.S. is also proposing tougher trade measures against Brazil, after imposing 25% tariffs in July over alleged unfair trade practices amid tensions between Trump and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The bottom line: Trump's tariff agenda is moving forward as Democrats in the incoming Congress look to curb presidential authority over trade policy and lower Americans' costs .

Russiaâs Vladimir Putin has been abandoned by one of the worldâs premier dictators amid a diplomatic loversâ tiff.
North Koreaâs Supreme Leader Kim Jong Un has furnished Moscow with its troops and munitions in the fight against Ukraine , with his soldiers clandestinely shipped west to the edge of Europe, where they fought inside Russiaâs borders to repel Kyivâs incursions and counterattacks.

But that backscratching has now ended, Ukrainian intelligence claims, after Pyongyang said it will cease military aid to Moscow.

Kim walks by a memorial to North Korean troops killed in Russia.
Ukraineâs Main Directorate of Intelligence said Thursday that North Koreaâs feathers were ruffled by Moscow when it proposed de-escalation in tensions between North Korea and South Korea.
Ukraine said that the halt order was personally issued by Kim.
Could the bromance be in danger?
According to the Kyiv Post , the order came after Andrey Rudenko, the Russian Deputy Foreign Minister, said that his country planned to seek de-escalation on the Korean peninsula.
North Korean Foreign Minister Choe Son-ui said Moscowâs request raised questions about alliances and relations with South Korea.
The two countries have a mutual agreement in place.

The withdrawal of ammunition poses a substantial problem for Moscow. Ukrainian intelligence said that ammo from the isolationist dictatorship accounted for between 25 percent and 40 percent of those used by Russia, according to a Kyiv Post report from July.
According to the Post, there is no suggestion that the existing troops drafted in to help Russia are being pulled away. Rather, Moscowâs request for additional troops, bumping numbers from 8,500 to 50,000, is being stalled.
North Korea has sent thousands of troops to assist Russia.
In 2025, Pyongyang acknowledged its troops had been deployed to help repel Ukraineâs Kursk offensive.
North Korea has also banned Russian military aircraft from its airspace, in addition to munitions withdrawals.
The two leaders have long aligned on the world stage.

South Korea is aligned with much of Europe and the West in its support for Ukraine and in its condemnation of Russia following its full-scale invasion in 2022.
However, South Koreaâs imports of Russian coal rose 35 percent in 2026 compared to last year, according to The Post.

articles.title_orig: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.title_zh: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that
articles.content_orig:
Andalusia, Spain – Surrounded by shelves heaving with canned goods and cured meats, the owners of a family-run grocery store are locked in a debate about Spain’s upcoming elections.
All politicians are “liars”, proclaims 32-year-old Antonio Cerezo, announcing he will cast a blank ballot. His cousin, Patricia Nicolas Cerezo, 43, is less certain, riddled with doubt about who to support.
As for her 18-year-old son, first-time voter Alfonso Duque, the only choice is the far-right Vox party : “It can’t get worse than this”.
The one thing that the family in the small village of Rioja seems to agree on is that Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez’s socialists must go.
A former socialist bastion, the southern region’s political landscape has changed. Since May’s regional election, it has been governed by a coalition of the conservative People’s Party (PP) and Vox, once a fringe party that has drawn support by championing migrant deportations and tapping into a wider wave of far-right, anti-establishment support across Europe.
Ahead of Sunday’s snap vote, observers say Andalusia’s political dynamics could offer a glimpse of what might come next nationally.
That arrangement could soon be tested at the national level.
Opinion polls put the PP first, followed by Sanchez’s Socialists (PSOE), with Vox third.
The PP is projected to fall short of an outright majority, but together the two right-wing parties are expected to have enough seats to govern.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo has indicated that he would prefer to lead a minority government with Vox’s backing in parliament, while leaving open the possibility of a coalition like the one in Andalusia.
Tucked away between rows of greenhouses and arid mountains in the southern region of Andalusia, Rioja is home to about 1,600 people.
Overlooking the plains framing the quaint village is a giant silhouette of a bull. For much of Francisco Franco’s dictatorship , this area remained poor and largely agricultural.
As machines took over more of the work in the fields, many Andalusians left for jobs in industrial centres such as Barcelona and Madrid. In the mid-seventies, the Socialists found fertile ground in a society that had long felt marginalised and neglected.
In 1982, the PSOE won an absolute majority in Andalusia’s first regional election, beginning a stretch in power that lasted more than three decades.
But by 2018, the Socialists’ hold on the southern region was starting to crack.
A series of corruption scandals tarnished the party’s image, benefitting the PP. The PSOE still came first in that year’s regional election, but the conservatives took power with the backing of the liberal Ciudadanos and Vox.
“For the first time, the PP opened the door to the far-right to be able to govern – that created a precedent for everything that happens today nationwide,” said Bosco Govantes, political science associate professor at Sevilla’s Universidad Pablo de Olavide. “Before, there was a red line, a stigma, over collaborating with the far right. But that move in Andalusia kicked off the normalisation of Vox’s narrative.”
The party was founded in 2013 when a group of ultraconservatives, led by Santiago Abascal, broke up with the conservatives they accused of being too indulgent towards Catalan separatists.
Vox at first struggled to get into the political mainstream, but entered Andalusia’s regional parliament in 2018.
Once the Catalan issue faded from the national debate, the party shifted its focus to migration.
Abascal accuses Sanchez of enabling what he calls “a migrant invasion” to “replace the Spanish people” as the Socialist government adopted an open-door policy and legalised undocumented migrants who had worked in Spain for years.
Since the start of Sanchez’s rule to last year, the number of foreign-born residents in Spain rose from 6.3 million to 10.4 million, official figures show. He takes pride in the policy, as Spain’s GDP grew under his tenure.
Vox, the likely kingmaker that is expected to increase its vote share more than any other party compared with the 2023 elections, wants to reverse those policies.
Some observers say the conservative party has had to harden its discourse, such as calling for stricter measures against migrants, to stop haemorrhaging voters to its right.
Polling by Ipsos suggested up to 20 percent of Spaniards who voted for the PP in the 2023 elections intended to vote for Vox on Sunday.
Sanchez has pitched the election as a battle between progress and regression, warning that PP and Vox “only agree when it comes to cutting back rights”.
But that argument falls flat in parts of Andalusia, where some do not fear a Vox-PP deal.
“I don’t mind if Vox is in government,” said Rosaria, a 69-year-old retired housewife, while adjusting her white scarf with a red floral pattern. “The PP will keep them in check. It’s a party with vision and structure”.
Sanchez warns that Vox wants to roll back women’s rights.
The issue of gender violence divides the two parties.
Last year, the PP backed the renewal of Spain’s cross-party pact on gender-based violence.
Vox wants to repeal the 2004 gender-based violence law, which protects women from abuse by current or former partners. The party argues that the law discriminates against men and wants to replace it with legislation covering domestic violence regardless of the victim’s sex.
At an event against gender-based violence, Rioja’s PP mayor Olga Maria Gonzalez Jurado was asked how the two parties were getting on in government in Andalusia.
“I think it’s going well,” she said, but she deflected questions on whether the PP had hardened its stance on immigration to keep up with Vox.
In Andalusia, the two parties have been pushing for stricter housing rules for non-Spanish applicants.
Councils can already give people who live or work locally priority for subsidised housing, regardless of nationality. Last month, the two parties backed a non-binding motion urging Madrid to give Spanish citizens priority for subsidised housing and housing aid. Their regional coalition deal also pledges to give people with longstanding ties to Andalusia or Spain priority for public benefits and social housing.
In other regions, the two parties’ cooperation has reached classrooms and places of worship. Aragon dropped a school programme teaching Arabic and Moroccan culture this year and Andalusia is due to follow in 2027.
In the Murcia town of Jumilla, Muslims held Eid al-Fitr prayers in a car park after PP and Vox backed restrictions on the use of municipal sports facilities. The restrictions have drawn criticism over their impact on Muslim religious gatherings.
In Valencia, the parties backed a rule requiring meat served in school canteens to come from animals stunned before slaughter, which still allows halal meals that meet the requirement. In the Balearic Islands, they voted to send Spain’s Congress a bill to ban the burqa [full-face veils sometimes worn by Muslim women that hide the entire face, including eyes] and niqab [similar, but the eyes are visible] in public spaces.
Vox has called for the deportation of foreigners it says, among other grounds, also live on public benefits. This measure – to remove someone with a valid right to stay – has no equivalent in Europe.
The party’s policies have left migrants on edge.
Yudy Ramirez is from Colombia and entered Spain four years ago. For years, took care of her child while juggling two jobs as an in-house caregiver and fruit picker at a greenhouse in Almeria for five euros per hour.
In June, the 49-year-old finally received legal papers.
“Many of us are scared, because returning is not in the plans at the moment,” she said.
Still, not all migrants are targeted in the same way.
Vox’s rhetoric has an ethno-racial undertone which looks at Spanish-speaking foreigners coming from Latin America in more favourable terms as they belong to an Iberosphere which connects far-right movements in the Latin world whose centre is occupied by Vox.

articles.title_orig: Trump tells Putin to ‘pull back all military aggression’ as he tries for peace deal to end ‘complete bloodbath’ in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Trump tells Putin to ‘pull back all military aggression’ as he tries for peace deal to end ‘complete bloodbath’ in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
By ELINA SHIRAZI, US SENIOR POLITICAL REPORTER
Published: 12:26 EST, 26 November 2026 | Updated: 12:27 EST, 26 November 2026
President Donald Trump has revealed he personally pressed Vladimir Putin to halt Russian provocations across Europe in an urgent push to end the Ukraine conflict, warning that the ongoing war has become 'a complete bloodbath.'
Taking to Truth Social on Thursday following late-night talks with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago, the president disclosed what he told the Russian strongman during their recent face-to-face meetings in China .
The president said he urged Moscow to stand down 'in hopes that a deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly'.
The Truth Social posts followed a Wednesday night sit-down between Trump and Rutte at the President's Florida estate, which Trump dubbed 'the Southern White House '.
Trump reveals he 'spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all military aggression against territories throughout Europe'.
Although the president stopped short of specifying which areas of Europe were under threat, his remarks reflect mounting concern across the alliance over recent warfare tactics aimed at countries near Russia's periphery, such as Estonia, Poland and Denmark.
Smoke rises above residential buildings following a Russian air attack in Kyiv, on Thanksgiving day, amid the Russian invasion of Ukraine
The Truth Social posts followed a Wednesday night sit-down between Trump and Rutte at the President's Florida estate, which Trump dubbed 'the Southern White House'
President Donald Trump has revealed he personally pressed Russian President Vladimir Putin to halt Russian provocations across Europe in an urgent push to end the Ukraine conflict, warning that the ongoing war has become 'a complete bloodbath'
Taking to Truth Social on Thursday morning following late-night talks with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at Mar-a-Lago, the president disclosed what he told the Russian strongman during their recent face-to-face
'I really believe this is a strong possibility - Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, a complete bloodbath - and will be a Great Tribute to everyone!' Trump declared.
Trump says the talks were overall 'very impactful' and centered on the wars in Ukraine and Iran, alongside the current state of the NATO alliance.
'We also talked about, at length, the importance of Russia and Ukraine avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the War - and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the War, as rapidly as possible,' Trump stated.
Calls from Trump for an immediate ceasefire come alongside the mounting toll of Russia's nearly five-year war in Ukraine.
Approaching five years since Russia's February 2022 full-scale invasion, the war has resulted in massive casualties, at least 490,000 confirmed Russian military deaths and up to 150,000 estimated Ukrainian losses, while peace efforts stall alongside heavy combat and rejected local ceasefires.
Following the recent meeting with Rutte, Trump also highlighted allied defense efforts, commending what he described as 'tremendous progress' in NATO military spending and production.
In a public statement, Trump also touted domestic weapons manufacturing, asserting that US output of military equipment and munitions has reached an all-time high.
Once American stockpiles, which he referred to as the nation's military 'cupboard,' are fully replenished, Trump said America's allies and partners around the world would 'be benefitting greatly.'

Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.
The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.
Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.
The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.
Nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.
U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes."
"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he said.
U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute.
Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

articles.title_orig: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.title_zh: Germany: 2 suspected Islamists arrested in Heidelberg and Cologne, suspected of plotting synagogue attack
articles.content_orig:
Germany 's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro- Iranian terrorist group.
It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne , several hours' drive to the north.
Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.
Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing.
After two suspects were arrested, Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia , thanked the security agencies for their vigilance and dedication. "Protecting Jewish life is our shared responsibility," he wrote on X.
"Jewish life must be able to flourish freely and safely in our country. Anyone who attacks it attacks us all," Wüst added.
Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization.
They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran .
Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025."
Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks."
"On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out."
Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency , the BfV.
More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation.
Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention.
One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it.
The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran.
These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9 , which caused property damage but no injuries.
Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later . An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after , prompting heightened security across the Netherlands.
In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March , not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism.
Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

articles.title_orig: Regional relations, modern munitions will poise U.S. to defeat China, Trump pick to lead Navy says
articles.title_zh: Regional relations, modern munitions will poise U.S. to defeat China, Trump pick to lead Navy says
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, views the tariff proposals as a pressure point on Southeast Asian economies and their trade relations with the U.S. and China.
She says that many of the region’s economies see a lot of Chinese goods pass through before heading to the U.S. market, with tariffs intended to “make it more difficult for economies like Vietnam to position themselves as collector economies between the U.S. and China,” she tells TIME.
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Overall, the proposed rates are just “one more complication in the relationship with the U.S.” that global partners have to contend with, adds Demarais.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: I test headphones for a living. These are the 12 best Black Friday AirPods deals
articles.title_zh: I test headphones for a living. These are the 12 best Black Friday AirPods deals
articles.content_orig:
If you purchase an independently reviewed product or service through a link on our website, Rolling Stone may receive an affiliate commission.
It’s been a big year for audio releases, with major players like Apple, Beats, Bose, Sennheiser, and Sony all dropping new models. While a pair of flagship headphones can cost a premium, Black Friday deals are here. Many of the best headphones on the market are getting discounts, including models that were released just months ago.
Best of all, most of these Black Friday deals are on headphones we’ve tested, including our favorite travel headphones , styles for the gym , and noise-canceling cans . We’ve also included deals on wireless earbuds if you’re more partial to in-ear styles.
There are admittedly a lot of deals to sift through, so these are a few that are especially worth it:
You can check out the best Black Friday headphone and earbud deals below, organized by brand.
The Space 2 headphones are a great option if you’re looking for budget noise-canceling headphones, and they’re under $100.
In our testing, Anker’s Liberty 5 Pro earbuds lived up to the bold claim of delivering the best voice-calling performance, particularly in loud environments. They’re available for $130 during Black Friday.
The second-gen AirPods Max headphones impressed us with great noise-canceling and the most impressive transparency mode of any over-ear headphones. They’re pricey, but discounted right now.
When we tested the AirPods Pro 3, we found that they were a worthy upgrade over the second-gen, thanks to the better noise-canceling and improved fit. They’re $100 off right now.
The Beats 360 headphones quickly became our favorites for gym use, thanks to the removable, replaceable fabric earcups and headband. The brand new headphones are already $100 off.
If you’re looking for workout earbuds, the Powerbeats Fit are one of the best options thanks to the tactile controls and in-ear wings that keep them in place.
Bose’s QuietComfort Ultra headphones deliver exceptional comfort and noise-canceling, plus handy features like an auto-sleep mode when you set them down.
The QuietComfort Ultra earbuds feature the top-tier noise-canceling Bose is known for, and they’re comfortable enough for all-day wear.
You can get a small discount on Bowers & Wilkins flagship headphones , which feature Nappa leather and aluminum details and high-performance audio and noise-canceling.
The Px7 S2e maintains the high-end performance of Bowers & Wilkins’ other headphones in a more affordable package.
Nothing’s over-ear headphones feature a quirky but stylish design, solid audio quality, and fun tactile controls. They’re $170 for Black Friday.
The Nothing Ear (a) earbuds are a great budget option, especially at this price. The case is compact and pocket-friendly, and the audio and noise-canceling performance is surprisingly solid for the price.
Sennheiser’s Momentum 5 over-ears were one of the most impressive headphone releases of the year. The noise-canceling was significantly improved over the last generation, and the over 50 hours of listening time is rare for headphones in this class.
The Momentum 5 may be an upgrade over the fourth-gen model, but you’d be hard-pressed to find Bluetooth headphones that sound this good for this price.
Sony’s WH-1000XM6 headphones feature great sound and noise-canceling, plus a dizzying number of features. The earcups are foldable, unlike on the XM5 model, making them more travel friendly.
Sony revived one of its most popular headphone styles with the XM4C, featuring a nearly identical build to the original while adding a few updated features.
Shokz’s earbuds are among our go-tos for runners; the open-ear design allows for awareness of your surroundings, and the secure fit stays put during workouts.
While Sonos’ newest Ace Ultra headphones aren’t on sale, the original Ace model is. You can pick them up for under $250.

articles.title_orig: Netherlands to Fight Rollout of Proposed US Curbs on ASML
articles.title_zh: Netherlands to Fight Rollout of Proposed US Curbs on ASML
articles.content_orig:
Export controls on chips and other technology shouldnât aim to cut China off completely â a strategy that will only backfire, warns Christophe Fouquet, CEO of ASML, the sole maker of the lithography machines needed to produce the worldâs most advanced AI chips.
âYou need [export controls] to protect very advanced technology, but you also have to use export control in such a way that you donât completely frustrate a country and invite that country to basically double down or triple down on development,â Fouquet said on Semaforâs Future Proof .
The debate over Chinese access to Western technology has intensified in Washington after revelations of Jensen Huangâs affair with a suspected Chinese spy left lawmakers divided on how aggressively to tighten curbs.
As a $520 billion de facto monopoly in chipmaking equipment, ASML sits at the center of that fight. Fouquet argued that continuing to sell China older equipment â ASMLâs shipments there are more than a decade behind the cutting edge â maintains a strategic âgeneration gapâ that keeps Beijing hooked on Western hardware rather than racing to build its own.
âFor almost 30 years, we have been able to keep an extremely high market share in China â very high means close to 100% â which means that they have accepted to rely on our technology with the idea that they had access to it,â Fouquet said.

articles.title_orig: Israel’s Eisenkot takes steps towards replacing Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Israel’s Eisenkot takes steps towards replacing Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
The Democrats froze talks earlier this week over Yashar's unity negotiations with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud
Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot and Democrats chairman Yair Golan reached an agreement in principle, looking to move forward in signing a coalition deal. The two parties announced the breakthrough hours after the two sides restarted talks.
The Democrats had halted negotiations earlier this week in protest of Yashar's contacts with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud on a unity government. However, Eisenkot confirmed Thursday morning that the talks were back on.
Under the understandings, the Democrats will receive four portfolios: "internal security in an expanded format," labor and welfare, communications, and culture and sports, which will include "a new administration for democracy." Golan is set to serve as internal security minister.
The party will also oversee the Ministry for Social Equality and chair the Knesset's Constitution Committee. One of its representatives will sit on the Judicial Selection Committee, and another will be the minister who links the government and the Knesset.
The Democrats noted that the agreements include a commitment to "fully cancel the regime coup," their term for the judicial overhaul, and to preserve "the independence of the judicial system."
The Democrats had asked for the justice portfolio but gave it up. "Our commitment to forming a government of change and our national responsibility require us to act quickly, reach agreements and also show a willingness to compromise," the party explained.
It added: "With this, we are paving the way to ending the Netanyahu government and saving Israeli democracy." The sides are still working on the final details before signing.
Earlier this week, Eisenkot and Yisrael Beitenu chairman Avigdor Lieberman also agreed to sign a coalition deal.

articles.title_orig: Staff at Grand Theft Auto VI developer vote against union recognition
articles.title_zh: Staff at Grand Theft Auto VI developer vote against union recognition
articles.content_orig:
Staff at the developer behind the Grand Theft Auto game franchise have voted against recognising a workplace union.
More than 1,500 workers at Rockstar, which has an office in Edinburgh, took part in the two-week ballot over formal recognition by the Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB).
The vote took place during an employment tribunal concerning a group of Rockstar staff who claim they were dismissed for trade union activities last year. Rockstar has denied this and alleged staff were sacked for discussing confidential information online.
About 75% of staff balloted voted against union recognition proposals, with 24.7% backing them.
The latest instalment in the long-running games franchise, Grand Theft Auto VI, was released last week .
It is thought to be one of the largest entertainment launches in history, attracting billions of pounds in its first seven days of sales.
IWGB said union recognition would have established a "formal framework" for staff to negotiate collectively with management over issues including pay, overtime compensation and bonuses, leave and pensions.
The union said it would also have allowed staff a right to consultation around some workplace changes, such as redundancies and the introduction of artificial intelligence.
It said the result of the ballot did not prevent workers from continuing to "push for workplace improvements" through the IWGB or joining the union.
"For anyone at Rockstar who believes in a fairer workplace, a fairer sector and a fairer society - this isn't a sign to retreat," staff represented by the union said.
"It's a sign to double down on what we stand for.
"Hundreds of our co-workers voted in favour of our union at Rockstar, yet sadly we recognise we have more work to do to build understanding and win the trust of more of our colleagues. We're ready to put in the effort to make that happen."
The union is representing 23 workers in the employment tribunal , which finished hearing evidence on 18 November, the day before Grand Theft Auto VI was released.
About 34 people are believed to have been dismissed from Rockstar North in October 2025 across the UK and Canada over what the company described as "the sharing of confidential company information".
Jennifer Kolbe, head of publishing at Rockstar Games, said: "This result reflects our team's strong support for continuing the direct relationships, collaboration and open dialogue that have helped make Rockstar Games so innovative and strong.
"As we look ahead, we're excited to build on all we've accomplished together."

articles.title_orig: Trump Says He Asked Putin to End Russia’s Military Aggression Across Europe During China Talks
articles.title_zh: Trump Says He Asked Putin to End Russia’s Military Aggression Across Europe During China Talks
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
US President Donald Trump says he has told Russian leader Vladimir Putin to “pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe ” in the hope this could lead to a quick settlement of the war in Ukraine.
“During my conversations in China with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia , I spent a lot of time talking about the fact that I would like to see President Putin pull back all Military aggression against territories throughout Europe, in the hopes that a Deal can be made between Russia and Ukraine, and made quickly,” Mr Trump wrote in a Truth Social Post.
“I really believe this is a strong possibility – Thousands of people are being killed each and every month, A COMPLETE BLOODBATH.”
The US president has frequently urged a negotiated end to the war in Ukraine.
On Thursday, however, he used broader language about “territories throughout Europe”, without specifying what that meant.
Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine started in 2022, other countries occasionally have accused Russia of provocative behavior.
Poland, a Nato member, this week accused Russia of deliberately violating Polish airspace.
Estonia recently linked an arson attack to Russia's military intelligence service.
Mr Trump made headlines when he warmly greeted Russian leader Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during the Apec summit in China.
The commander-in-chief's enthusiastic reception of Mr Putin was condemned by commentators and former diplomats who labelled it an embarrassment for America.
Former US ambassador to Russia Michael McFaul said that his decision to call Mr Putin his “friend” was radically out of step with American society.
Back at the White House, Mr Trump was asked whether Mr Putin was also a friend to the United States.
“I can't speak to America,” he replied, while emphasising his “very good” personal relationship with the Russian leader.
He later posted an image of himself standing close to Mr Putin and shaking his hand beneath a caption in large type: “My Friend.”
It was one of dozens of photos he shared from the summit throughout the course of the day, many of which depicted him alongside the Russian leader and Chinese President Xi Jinping .
